Entering the hall, after the attendant had finished burning incense, the Master pointed to the attendant and said, "The attendant has already preached the Dharma for everyone.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he drew a circle with both hands, then spread his legs apart and pressed his knees together, saying: "The whole lump cannot be split;
three people share only two bodies. There is truly no flavor to be found; who can swallow it? If you can swallow it, then do so.
But as for those who cannot swallow it—do not act recklessly."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Wishing to speak, words fail; beneath the forest trees, let us deliberate well. But tell me, how shall we deliberate?
At times one gathers wild vegetables and boils them with their roots; one hews fresh firewood and burns it with its leaves."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The old woman selling fans shields herself from the sun with her hand; Mr. Tian wears his trousers so high they do not reach his knees.
The headless boatman lets the wind carry him along; Last night, the whistles blew at the edge of the fence."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The hundred rivers have different currents, yet they all return to the sea; the myriad paths are distinct, yet they all enter this school.
He struck the meditation staff and said: "To heal a sore beneath the eye, one gouges out the flesh from the heart."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night at the third watch, suddenly the earth shook violently, causing Mount Sumeru to tremble and the waters of the ocean to boil.
Within it were infinite sentient beings, all in the midst of their dreams, unaware and unknowing, as if existing yet as if dead.
He struck the meditation staff and said, "Assembly, did you hear it? It nearly cost us our lives!"

Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat: As the autumn wind begins to stir, the sack’s mouth is opened. Those who come do so of their own accord; those who depart do so of their own accord.
From Jianghuai to Liangzhe, there is ample local tradition; from Mount Heng to Mount Lu, there is even more secluded charm. All rushing about and spinning in circles.
Through kalpa after kalpa, amidst the waves of samsara, you must know that the Tathāgata Acalanātha has never taken a single step.
But tell me, how do you express this "not taking a step"? After a long silence, he said: "Just now he came from the hall; now he returns to the hall."
One day he ascended the hall. As soon as he stepped out of the Dharma Hall, the assembly offered their greetings, and he returned directly to his quarters.
He then ascended the hall again and said: "Is the Way far away? It is true in every encounter. The Master said: "Cool breezes and bright moon;
green mountains and white clouds. "Is the Sage far away? To embody him is to attain the divine. The Master said: "Leaping about upon the eyebrows; hidden within the eyelashes."
[The Master] patted the meditation seat and said: "A distant relative is not as good as a neighbor nearby.
He ascended the hall and said: "Let them slander; let them be wrong. To carry fire to burn the heavens is but a weary toil for oneself.
When I hear it, it is like drinking nectar; it melts away and enters suddenly into the inconceivable. Great assembly, even Yongjia still has this remaining."

At Zifu Temple in Zhenzhou, the Master ascended the hall. Pointing to the seat, he said, "This is the Dharma-seat of Zifu; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, such a favorable opportunity is difficult to encounter.
Do not let it pass. He then ascended the seat. Once the assembly was settled, the Master asked, "Do you understand?
If you do not know how to be a guest, you trouble the host. Thereupon, he descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Above is heaven; below is earth. North, south, east, and west each abide in their respective positions.
Yet there was a time when Baoning turned heaven into earth and turned earth into heaven; he called east west and called south north, twisting the nostrils around.
"Exchange skulls! Among you, there are those who share the same death and the same life; why not come forward? Let everyone lend a hand—is there anyone?
After a long silence, he said: "When serving as an official, do not draw near; when acting as a guest, do not fall behind."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
Now tell me, what treasure is this? It is neither blue, yellow, red, nor white; it possesses none of the characteristics of male or female. What words are these? Nevertheless, even so..."
One side is insufficient; the other side has a surplus. Ascending the hall:
this very seeing and hearing is not seeing and hearing. There are no further sounds or forms to present to you. If one understands within this, there is absolutely nothing to be done;
essence and function may be distinguished or not, without any hindrance. Baoning once took his staff as the essence. At times...
At that time, the staff serves as the function; it acts as the essence (*tī*). Heaven and earth are silent;

the world is serene—this is the function. Autumn changes into winter’s withering; spring gives birth and summer grows—do you not see that within the essence there is function, and within function there is essence?
Essence does not depart from function, and function does not depart from essence. Holding the staff horizontally, he says: "Tell me, is this the essence or the function? If you reach the various...
[The Master] said, "Do not say that Baoning’s four-edged staff is merely a flat piece of wood.
[He] ascended the hall, held up his staff, and said: 'This is what Yunmen, Linji, Deshan, and Yantou used throughout their entire lives without exhausting it.
Now it is in Baoning’s hands; it is not worth half a penny. Nevertheless, it is still quite useful.'"
"Venerable may become base. But tell me: where is that which is venerable and where is that which is base?
He threw down his staff and descended from the seat. At Changlu, he ascended the hall and said: "Before you have arrived here, nothing is spoken of. Now that you have arrived here, how is it so?"

"You have a mouth and a tongue; what prevents you from speaking nonsense? Let anyone who has a question come forward. When no one responded to his repeated summons, the Master said, "You still have some merit.
Ancient Zifu said: "If you see the monastery flagpole of Zifu from across the river, turn back immediately.
I would give twenty blows to such a person's heels. Baoning said: "Yesterday I left Jinling, took a small boat across the Great River, and arrived at the gate of Changlu."
Descending, he saw the pagoda pole and observed the Buddha hall. He went up to the abbot’s quarters and paid his respects to Master Zu-yin.
The Master did not reprimand him for his offenses but treated him with exceptional kindness. Why was this? "The grace is so deep that words fail; what is held in the heart is naturally clear.

The Master then ordered him to ascend the seat before the assembly. Unable to avoid it, he spoke in a jumble of foreign and Chinese tongues, deceiving everyone—this was because he did not recognize the difference between good and evil.
There is yet another verse: "Riding the momentum, I sail my small boat with ease; in an instant, the wind carries me to the riverhead.
I know not what we shall discuss upon meeting—Virtuous Elders, try and say it!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "It has hands and feet, yet it has no front or back; those with clear eyes cannot see it. Heaven revolves to the left, and earth turns to the right.
He patted his knee and said: "A gust of west wind comes, and two or three leaves fall."
Ascending the hall, the Master said: "The ancients said: 'Those who enter through the gate of Mañjuśrī—walls, bricks, and rubble—will trigger your awakening for you.

Those who enter through the gate of Avalokiteśvara—frogs and earthworms—will trigger your awakening for you. Those who enter through the gate of Samantabhadra—without moving a step, they pervade the ten directions.

Great assembly, from east, west, south, and north, from the four intermediate points and above and below, wherever you strike or bump against things, you do not realize it and do not know it; this is a transgression."
"Where is it? After a long silence, he said: "With rouge and powder, one can easily become a beautiful woman; without money, it is difficult to be a fine young man. He ascended the hall and said:
"The Yellow-Faced Old Man appeared in the world, piling up bones on level ground. The Blue-Eyed Barbarian came from the West, raising waves where there was no wind.
Those who approach cinnabar turn red; those who approach ink turn black. Linji and Yunmen have only entangled branches and led out vines. Baoning..."
There are also immeasurable transgressions. All of you also have immeasurable transgressions. Do you understand this thoroughly? After a long silence, he said:
"The face wrinkles only because one accompanies others in laughter; the back becomes hunched because one has been struck many times. *Chan*."
Ascending the hall, he said: "It cannot be known by wisdom; it cannot be cognized by consciousness. The path of language is severed; the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Baoning says:
It can indeed be known by wisdom, and it can indeed be cognized by consciousness. The path of language is not severed; the sphere of mental activity is not extinguished. Why?
The green mountains only know how to polish the past and present; the flowing water has never washed away right and wrong."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wind whistles through the branches; the rain breaks the clods of earth. At dawn, the sound of orioles on the pillow is shattered.
Frogs and earthworms cry out all at once. Miaode and Śāriputra do not understand it at all. They do not understand it at all. Three form a flock; four make a troop."
Deep and mysterious; light and ethereal. Moving toward the north, south, east, and west, he plucks the *li* flowers and *li* blossoms.
One girdle, then two girdles, as he ascends the hall.
At all times he raises them; everywhere he speaks of them. There is no taboo, no cessation. Holding his staff crosswise, he asks: "Do you understand?"
A rain of falling blossoms throughout the night; the flowing waters of the city are filled with fragrance.
*Pa! A single strike.* Descends from the seat. Ascending the hall on New Year’s Day: Yesterday, last year departed; today, this year arrives. Did last year depart, or did it not?
Does this year arrive, or does it not? Snow a foot deep fills the wilds; across the great earth, not a speck of dust remains. The person without name or character—raise it up!
My eyes wander aimlessly.

The Transformation Master ascends the hall: upon his body he wears robes offered by the faithful, and from his mouth he eats food offered by the faithful. Yet the giver leaves not even a trace of a hair’s breadth behind, and the receiver leaves no footprint.
The Great Gate of Generosity stands wide open; hundreds of thousands, even billions of offerings, are grasped and brought forth with a single stroke of the hand.
Be careful not to seek it from another. Since you do not seek it from another, speak forth a single phrase from where your hand naturally rests.
Is there one? If not, Baoning shall speak for himself: "A single letter conveys the news;
two servings of tea express the ritual of sincerity."

Question: “Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests thousands, tens of thousands, and billions of bodies. From time to time he appears to people of his own era, yet the people themselves do not recognize him.
Does the Master recognize him? Answer: “I do not recognize him. The monk said: “The stone ox frequently spits forth mist for three springs;
the wooden horse’s neighing fills the roads. Answer: “Even if you miss it, you still do not know. The monk asked: “What is it like to miss it?”
The Master then gave a shout. The monk joined his palms and said, "A true spiritual friend. The Master replied, "I am mindful that you were formerly the *karmadāna*.

[The monk] asked about the gesture of Vimalakīrti spreading his palm, whereupon the world appeared vast and majestic, and the snapping of fingers by Sudhana, whereupon the pavilions appeared in infinite layers.

"Is this the wondrous function of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), or is it the nature of the fundamental substance (*dharmatā*)? The Master replied, "Neither is it so. The monk asked, "Then how is it? The Master replied, "Sprinkling water."
“[The monk] does not grasp it. The monk said, “The soldiers follow the seal; the generals pursue the talisman. The Master replied, “A thousand miles, ten thousand miles.
The monk said, “I am just like this; how about you, Master? The Master replied, “You are a wandering monk. The monk said, “Thirty years from now, someone will bring this up.
The Master said, “Keep this in mind. Question: “When the Master ascends the jeweled throne and the fourfold assembly faces the dais, [what is] the direct [point]?”
[The monk] said, "From the West you have come; please grant us a proclamation. He replied, "Two slow, three fast. The monk said, "Today’s assembly is no empty affair.
He replied, "Every beat is a command. The monk clapped his hands and said, "La-la-li! He replied, "That too is like one who knows the sound. The monk said, "The benefactor has received grace;
this student bows in thanks. He replied, "The wind stirs and the grass moves. The monk asked, "As for the principle that transcends [the ordinary]..."
[The Master] did not answer. [A monk asked: "What is the meaning of 'entering the marketplace with hands hanging down'? [The Master] replied, "Both feet planted firmly on the ground.
The monk said, "All beings, including devas and humans, receive this power of grace. [The Master] replied, "The nostrils reach up to the heavens. The monk bowed; the Master said, "Do not move it.
[Another monk] asked, "What is one who is at ease amidst the dust of the world? [The Master] replied, "While walking, it does not hinder one from swinging the arms. [Another monk] asked, "What is..."
The Great Meaning of the Buddha-Dharma. Answer: In the cauldron of boiling water, there is no place that is not hot.
Ascending the hall after leaving the monastery: To dangle precariously atop a hundred-foot pole is for a person on level ground to knit their brows in distress.
Now, in my decrepit old age, I have become useless; who shall follow in these former footsteps? If there is anyone who can attain the Way, try and say it! Liang.
Jiuyun said: "If there were no one to speak of this Way, it would not be as well to entrust it to Prefect Xie; having finished addressing the assembly, he spoke again:
'This national monastery is a premier site among the famous sites of the realm. By fortunate circumstance, I have continued my cultivation here.

My illusory body is already burdened by many ailments, and snow-white hair is soon to cover my entire head. A hundred years in this floating world are still not enough; even a thousand turns of a whirlwind would hardly suffice.'"
"Today morning, I joyfully become a guest of the immortals; following my nature, I roam at ease and attain freedom.
He then bestows the certificate and ascends the hall. He claps his hands three times, points to his mouth, and wiggles his hand three times. He then descends from the seat.
The head of the city-ward requests entry into the hall. The chamber of Makka is not closed; the gate of the Abbot’s quarters opens once more.

To those who do not begrudge their eyebrows, he extends his body and invites them to enter. The monk steps forward, claps his hands three times, points to his mouth, and wags his hand three times, asking: "How is it?"
[The Master] replied, “It is still slightly off. The monk said, “Though you open your mouth from beginning to end, what can you do against Heaven? [The Master] replied, “You have seen through me.
The monk shook his hand three times and returned to the assembly. [The Master] remarked, “A fine *śrāmaṇera*!
[The Master] asked, “One plays with peril atop a hundred-foot pole; such a person frowns even on level ground. Now that the brows are already spread, what is it to play with peril?”
[The Master] said, "It depends entirely on clapping hands. The monk said, "Turning over—truly there is a reason for this. [The Master] replied, "Look for yourself.
The monk said, "What if one suddenly falls? [The Master] replied, "Agh! The monk said, "I want everyone to know this too. [The Master] replied, "..."
When water is level, it does not flow; when a person is equanimous, they do not speak. The monk said, "When one has spirit, one adds to that spirit. The Master let out a single sigh.
The monk asked, "When one wishes to retire from a famous monastery but cannot take leave, and the Dharma-vehicle must be sung again—how is this? Answer: "Leaves fall and return to the root.
The monk said, "The Wheel of Dharma turns once more upon Jambudvīpa; the light of the Way shines again for a thousand years. Answer: "Spring has come."
The sprouts emerge as before. A monk said, "The dew and rain bestow their grace; all sentient beings rely upon them. He replied, "There is no idle person in the great earth.
Then he said, "In the cycle of the three realms and six paths, the karmic mirror leaves nothing hidden—neither beauty nor ugliness. There is no need to linger further on the affairs of others;
it is entirely what one has done oneself that one must receive. Now, within each of you, there is a face of karma for yourselves."
A mirror. It is vividly clear. Now tell me, is it beautiful or ugly? Try turning your head and looking at yourself.
Furthermore, an outsider asked the World-Honored One, "What Dharma should you preach today? The Honored One replied, "I shall preach the Dharma of concentration. The next day, he asked again.
"What Dharma do you teach? The Venerable said, "I teach the indeterminate Dharma. Daowu asked, "Why was it determinate yesterday? Why is it indeterminate today?

The Venerable said, "Yesterday it was determinate; today it is indeterminate. O worthy ones, you should know that in the Buddha-dharma there is no fixed characteristic, nor is there a characteristic of non-fixity.
It is established according to the capacity [of the recipient] and applied according to the occasion. At any given time, one may speak of existence, and one may also speak of non-existence."
It may be attained through fixed [dharmas], it may be attained through the teaching of the fixed, and it may also be attained through the unfixed. It is like the vast void:
expansive and unobstructed, allowing for any manner of penetration, free and sovereign in every direction. Suppose someone were to ask Baoning today, "What Dharma should you preach?"
He would simply say, "I am teaching the indeterminate dharma. If asked on the following day, "What dharma did you teach? he would say, "I taught the determinate dharma.
Or if asked, "Why was it indeterminate yesterday, and why is it determinate today? he would simply say, "Yesterday it was indeterminate; today it is determinate."
Someone asked, "What about yesterday’s state of non-fixation? He replied, "I have not yet finished my second expression of gratitude to the Prefect.
Someone asked, "What about today’s state of fixation? He replied, "The market households have already prepared the tea ceremony, and the expressions of gratitude are complete.
He then said: "Retiring to lead a hidden life—my will was not to follow it. In this world, where could I find a place to be accepted? As before, I return once more to the dust of the world."
The mud is cleared away; in every thing and at every head, the ancestors are revealed.
[He] strikes the meditation seat and descends from the seat. Entering the hall: "Sakyamuni, the Old Man, preached the Dharma for forty-nine years without ever uttering a single word.
Upagupta filled his chamber with counting sticks yet never ordained a single person. Bodhidharma did not dwell in Shaoshi; the Sixth Patriarch..."
"If you do not dwell at Caoxi, who is the successor? Who is the one awakened first? Since he has no wound of his own, do not inflict injury upon him.
He clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying, "I am glad that all under heaven is at peace!"
Ascending the hall: When the myriad things are nourished by a single rain, the sprouts do not depart from the soil. A sweet melon is sweet all the way to its stem;

a bitter gourd is bitter down to its roots. Ascending the hall: From morning until evening, I have spoken horizontally and vertically; yet, alas, I have never once touched so much as a single hair of his.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Do you understand? The first and third, the eleventh; the middle ninth and the final seventh. There is no need to ask about Tiangang or He Kui;
what need is there to speak of Daji or Xiaoji? He drew a line across and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he took up his staff, struck it once, and said, "Why do you not preach the Dharma?
He struck it a second time and said, "Vigilant, truly vigilant; clear, truly clear. Thirty years hence, you must not allow yourselves to be deceived.
He struck it a third time and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he called to the assembly. Pointing upward with his finger and then downward, he said, "This is Śākyamuni.
Raising his fist, he said, "This is Kāśyapa. Joining his palms, he said, "This is Ānanda. Spreading both hands wide, he asked, "What is this?
He replied, "It would put people to shame!"

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Lingyun attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms. He had a verse that said: "For thirty years I have sought the swordsman; How many times have leaves fallen and branches sprouted?
Since the moment I first beheld the peach blossoms, To this very day, I have no further doubt.

When Xuansha heard this, he said: "How perfectly true! How perfectly true! Yet I dare guarantee that you, elder brother, have not yet reached the ultimate. Now tell me, Lingyun— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with "Lingyun," indicating the sentence is incomplete.*
Yun, what principle do you see? Is it not that you have awakened to the principle that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, neither going nor coming, and are empty stillness?
If it were so, when did you ever awaken? As for Xuan Sha speaking thus—does he approve of him or does he not approve?
If you say he approves, where are Xuan Sha’s eyes? If you say he does not...
"Ken-ta. Where does Lingyun’s fault lie? There has been much deliberation among the assembly; thus, a thousand hearings are not equal to one seeing.
Baoning also dares to guarantee that you all have not yet reached the ultimate realization. Now, listen to this verse: Lingyun suddenly beheld the peach blossoms;
Fortunately he met Xuansha, a true master. This story shall never fall into oblivion through the ages; Let the clouds drift as they will."
The waters flow to the ends of the earth.
Entering the hall for instruction, [the Master] raised the following cases: Xuefeng said, "On the South Mountain there is a turtle-nosed snake; all of you, look well!
Changqing said, "In the hall today, many will lose their lives. Xuansha said, "Using the South Mountain as..."

"Mo! Yunmen threw his staff toward Xuefeng’s face and made a gesture of fear. The Master picked up the staff, called to the assembly, and said, "Your very bodies and lives are lost! He then descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall: "This morning is the first day of the tenth month; the incense burner is crowded, yet there is no smoke or fire. Those who have shaved their heads and donned the black robes vie with one another to sit by the brazier.
The frost is clear and the sky has just grown cold; the water is chilly, but the ice has not yet frozen. Who else in heaven or among men could possibly surpass me?
He clapped his hands and laughed loudly, then descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "There is a fellow, strange and ugly, with eyes staring straight ahead and a nose as sharp as a blue awl. Facing south, he gazes at the Big Dipper;
he knows how to make the golden crow cry at midday and the iron ox bellow at midnight. Heaven and earth spin, mountains and rivers run; the feathered tribes and hairy multitudes lose their way.
It reaches the point where Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra emerge here and vanish there, leaping freely in every direction—ten thousand lives, ten thousand deaths."
Receiving [this teaching], he suddenly encountered that Yellow-Faced Gautama, who, not sparing his own eyebrows, repeatedly rubbed the crown of his head and bestowed upon him a prophecy, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You perform great Buddha-work! Rare indeed, rare indeed!

Thereupon, he himself rubbed and stroked [his head], trembling with fear and anxiety, hiding his head and shrinking back his hands. O Great Assembly, this story has already spread; why wait for the third [turning of the wheel]?
Ten years later, he ascended the hall and said:
"Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad dharmas are one body with me. He held up his staff and said:
"The whole household pays no heed to matters of rise and fall; they only know how to dwell amidst the clouds upon Lake Dongting."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When we meet, no brow is raised; you go east, and I go west.
Crimson clouds pierce the blue sea; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. Baoning does not do so; neither west nor east, meeting one another everywhere.
The ears stand out straight, the hair is disheveled. Laughing aloud at heaven, pointing at empty space—what is this? The cold wind whistles, the fine rain mists."

Mong. Entering the hall, he said: "The Dharma-thunder resounds; the Dharma-drum is struck. Benevolent clouds are spread to sprinkle sweet dew. The Dharma-thunder has already resounded; the Dharma-drum has already been struck.
Benevolent clouds gather in dense masses; sweet dew falls in torrents. The myriad species and thousands of spirits all receive its benefit. Its...
The benefit is already vast, yet its merit remains unmanifested. As for this non-manifestation: when the Way flourishes, it does not transmit imperial edicts;
when the times are serene, one ceases singing songs of great peace.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Great Square has no exterior; the Great Circle has no interior. With neither interior nor exterior, saints and ordinary beings are gathered together.
Gravel and rubble emit light; Mount Sumeru is pulverized. The infinite Dharma gates and hundreds of thousands of samādhis—hold up his staff and says:
"All are right here. Do you understand? *Suru suru, siri siri*."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The true reality is formless; yet it manifests forms and reveals appearances. A thousand wonders and ten thousand shapes are made manifest from this.

When joyful, light radiates across the face; when angry, the two brows stand abruptly erect. Neither ordinary nor holy, sometimes right and sometimes wrong, humans cannot fathom them and heaven cannot measure them.
If you grasp this directly, you are not yet called a man of worth. If you do not turn your head when called, then do not even try."
A misunderstanding. Ascending the hall, he said: "The sun may grow cold; the moon may grow hot. No demons can destroy the True Teaching. Baoning, however, says it is not so:
"The moon may grow cold; the sun may grow hot. Even the demons can destroy the True Teaching. What, then, is the True Teaching? The tide.
In the fields, rice is sown and the harvest is bountiful; on the village roads, half the people one meets are monks.

Ascending the hall, the Master said: "To understand speech is not a matter of the tongue; to be able to speak is not the sound itself. When the hundred members of the body all disintegrate, there remains one thing that eternally abides as the numinous spirit.
The Master snapped his fingers and said, "O assembly! Upon the blue heavens, further misery and suffering are added."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If he comes from the bright side, strike him on the bright side. He clapped his hands once. "If he comes from the dark side, strike him on the dark side.
He clapped his hands once. "If he comes from all four directions and the eight points, strike him with a continuous barrage. He clapped his hands once. "What if he does not come in any of these ways?
He shouted: "It will make the bystanders laugh to death!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly refrain from speaking. To speak is for horns to grow.
Great assembly, the horns have grown! Is it an ox? Is it a horse?"

At the Zhijia Monastery, he ascended the hall and said: "Cease speaking of causes and conditions; this is not the proper occasion. A lone horse and a single spear—cutting through nails and slicing through iron.
A monk asked: "Those who do good cannot praise them enough; those who do evil cannot lament them enough.

But as for those who neither do good nor do evil, what then? The Master replied: "Calling out to heaven, there is no response; calling out to the earth, there is no hearing. The monk... [remained silent].
[The Master] said, "On the tower of Yueyang, I saw many boatmen hoisting their sails. The monk replied, "Those who understand are few.
The monk drew a single line with his sitting cloth (*zuoju*). The Master then shouted. The monk also shouted. The Master said, "You have missed it, yet you do not even know it.

The monk said, "My acquaintances fill the world. [The Master] replied, "Prostrate yourself! The monk responded with an assent. The Master then struck him. He asked, "Among all these guests from the four seas gathered in the hall, each one..."
"Study non-action (*wuwei*). I do not yet understand how one studies non-action. The Master replied, "What would you have me tell you, monk?

The monk said, "All worthies and sages take the dharma of non-action as their standard; why then are there differences among them? The Master replied, "A fan of blue silk provides no breeze or coolness.
The monk said, "May the great assembly bear witness. This student bows in thanks. The Master replied, "As for bowing in thanks—"
[The Master] said, “I have attained it. [The monk] asked, “To cut straight to the root is what the Buddhas have certified; to pluck leaves and seek branches is not for me.

Setting aside for now the matter of plucking leaves and seeking branches, what is the matter of cutting straight to the root? [The Master] answered, “A mosquito on an iron ox. The monk said, “I have now understood the matter of cutting straight to the root.
But how do you instruct those of middling and inferior capacity? [The Master] answered, “Sweat flows down the spine of the stone man.”
[The Master] said, "The donor has received the grace; this student bows in thanks. [The Master] replied, "Thirty years from now, these words will spread widely. He then said:
"The true mandate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs leaves both ordinary and holy beings behind. It is difficult to clarify through intellectual wit; mind and境 (objects) are both severed.
Therefore, when Buddhas and Patriarchs arrive here, they all lose their sharpness and are rendered tongue-tied. Should there be even a single word or half-sentence, it is entirely for the sake of..."
The saying of "the snake drawing legs" is fundamentally non-existent within the reality of ultimate principle.

Why do you say that people must simply have a sudden flash of insight, not follow after words and phrases, return to the root and source, avoid wandering onto bypaths, trample through the illusory city, sever the two extremes, and sit upright once they have returned home?
Why do you people not look back to the time before the Buddha appeared?
Apprehend it at the moment of this worldly time. Apprehend it before the Patriarch arrived. Apprehend it before your parents were born.
Now, when your parents had not yet been born, what face did you have? Do you understand thoroughly? After a long silence, he said:
"The ancient mirror is perfectly round and free from even the slightest blemish; I pray you, turn your head and take a look."
Ascending the hall: Last night the earthen ox bellowed; this morning the wooden horse gallops. Striking the stone Buddha of Jiazhou, he startles the barbarian monk of Shaoshi.
The barbarian monk’s front teeth are missing; with his mouth agape toward people, how can he speak?
Early spring in the first month is still cold; it is not yet the scorching heat of midsummer.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised an old precedent: An elder arrived at Linji and asked, "Is bowing right? Or is not bowing right? Linji gave a shout. The elder bowed.
Linji said, "This thief! The elder said, "This thief! and departed. Linji remarked, "Do not say it was nothing."
The Head Seat stood to one side. Jì said, "Tell me, is there a fault here or not? The Seat replied, "There is. Jì said, "Is it on the part of the guest or the part of the host?

The Seat replied, "Both have it. Jì said, "Where does the fault lie? The Seat then departed. Jì said: *Note: This passage is from the *Wumenguan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 18, concerning the encounter between Master Linji Yixuan and his Head Seat.*

He neither eliminates delusive thoughts nor seeks the Truth. Ho! Ho! The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature. Washing soil in the mud. The illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma."
To add a point to an arrow already lodged in one’s body—this very moment, if you were to turn back, you would have already abandoned your home and dispersed your affairs.
Yet, if you continue to rush forward, alas, the mountains are heavy and the waters are far.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When people scold one another, there are no good words; when they strike one another, there are no good fists. Great assembly, you must act in this way before you can succeed.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "When a false person preaches the True Dharma, the True Dharma is entirely false. When a true person preaches false dharma, the false dharma is entirely true.
Raising his staff, he said: "Is this false? Is this true? *Du!* Where is this place where one speaks of the false or the true?
He then cast the staff down and said: "Feel free to take this and present it to all quarters."

The monk said, "There is not even a word that permits one's own emergence. The Master replied, "The official does not detest deception.
The monk drew a circle. The Master then shouted. The monk also shouted. The Master again drew a circle. The monk made a single stroke with his sitting mat. The Master said, "Thirty years hence."
[The Master] said, "Do not misquote. The monk said, "The spring breeze continues to disturb without ceasing. [The Master] replied, "Do not show off so much.
He asked, "I do not ask about the mechanism of profound stillness; how is it to lower one's hand and enter the marketplace? [The Master] replied, "Countless people add feet to a snake."
The monk said, "Last night a cold wind arose from the eight directions; this morning the flowing waters have risen in the front creek.
He replied, "The Sixth Patriarch could not read characters. The monk drew the shape of a half-moon and asked, "Tell me, what is this?

The Winter Solstice. A monk asked: "The donors look up in reverence; the assembly from the four seas has gathered like clouds. Regarding the supreme vehicle of the ancestral lineage, we pray that the Master will proclaim it.
The Master replied: "This year the Son of Heaven pays homage at the Southern Suburb. The monk said: "When one person experiences joy, the myriad people depend upon it.

The Master replied: "The Golden Cock proclaims a great amnesty. The monk said: "I wonder, Master, whether I too have a share in this? The Master replied: "Do not say you do not receive the grace. The monk [bowed].
[The Master] said: "If one goes away just like this, what then? [The monk] replied: "A person of keen intelligence is hard to find. [The Master] asked: "Last year’s morning was the winter solstice;
this year is still last year’s year. The two wheels interact and flow constantly; when one reaches this state, how can one discuss 'non-transmigration'?
[The Master] replied: "The sky is cold and the days are short. The monk said: "Why do you change the old and replace it with the new? [The Master] replied: "Deep in winter, there is much [to do]."
"Snow and rain—this must surely be a year of plenty. The monk said, "The wild fire cannot burn it all away; when the spring breeze blows, it grows again.
The Master replied, "When will there ever be an end to this? The monk said, "Every drop is the sound of autumn. The Master replied, "In the end, it does not fall anywhere else.
The monk gave a single sweep with his sitting mat (*zuoju*). The Master let out a long sigh.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The single moon universally appears in all waters; all waters and moons are subsumed within the single moon. The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature;
my nature is identical and merges with that of the Tathāgata. Raising one's head, one touches the crown of Vipaśyin; lowering one's feet, one treads upon the feet of Maitreya.
Picking up the spoon and grasping the chopsticks, one manifests billions of transformation bodies; changing the water and adding incense, one acts as an eternal [Buddha]."
The Buddha-works as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are neither "sublime functions" nor "supernatural powers. In principle, nothing is not perfect; in phenomena, nothing is not complete.
If you can awaken to this, whose hearth will ever lack smoke? If you have not yet reached this state, then illness is the excellent medicine for sentient beings.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Without destroying conventional designations (*prajñapti*), one speaks of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). He held up his staff and said, "This is a conventional designation.
Which one is the ultimate reality? He struck the ground once and said, "This is the ultimate reality. Which one is the conventional designation?
Those with eyes stepped forward; those without eyes withdrew.

Ascending the hall, he reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs; shameless and without remorse, he preached the Dharma as non-Dharma and non-Dharma as Dharma, possessing the great icchantika nature and repudiating cause and effect.
Now tell me: is this man heterodox or orthodox? After a long silence, he said: "If he is heterodox, he is entirely heterodox;
if he is orthodox, he is entirely orthodox."
Ascending the hall, he said: "He comes! He comes! After a long silence, he said: "He goes! He goes! Ascending the hall again, he said:
"I have long kept this essential matter in silence, not wishing to speak of it hastily. He called to the assembly: "Who among you is willing to find rest before death?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The feet are thin, yet the straw sandals are wide; the hair is long, and the monk’s appearance is ugly.
He called to the assembly, saying: "Two ghostly eyes protrude forth; there is also a pair of hands for a beggar."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Gold cannot buy gold; water cannot wash water. Old Guizhi of Yangqi—when you try to fathom him, there is no principle.
There being no principle, he knocks out the teeth right in front of your face."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Taking the sutras to discuss in the temple, carrying water to sell by the riverhead—it all does not even amount to a single copper coin.
It puts that newly ordained monk of the 'Yellow Head' to shame."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The ancients said, 'Members of the monastic community must be given their proper portion of fodder before they will do.
Now, what is this proper portion of fodder for a member of the monastic community? After a long silence, he said: 'Three meals a day is not considered much.'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor excess. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one falls short.
When the ancients spoke thus, they truly outshone the past and surpassed all who came after. Nevertheless, even so, one cannot help but provide a forced analysis."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "I see those who deceive themselves, like one carrying a basket of water while running. Once they reach home in a single breath, what has ever been in the basket?
Clapping his hands and laughing loudly, he said: 'When there is spirit, add more spirit; where there is no elegance, there too is elegance.'"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The power of inconceivable liberation—its wondrous functioning is as boundless as the sands of the Ganges.
He struck his staff once and said: "The Dharmakāya has been swallowed up. Where will you all go to avoid it?

If you can speak, then even before a precipice of ten thousand fathoms there is a path for the living. If you cannot speak, then the dead on the great earth are as numerous as hemp and millet. He struck [the staff] once.
Descend. Descend from the seat. Ascend to the hall.
Leveling the path and knocking at the gate—these were all traversed by those ancients, moving freely in every direction.
Where, then, can Baoning plant his feet? Do you understand thoroughly? The mountains and rivers cannot be fully traversed; rain and snow continue to fall.
At no fixed time, he ascended the hall and said: "Whether it be right or wrong, people do not recognize it; whether it be acting against or with the flow, heaven cannot fathom it.
O Great Assembly, what is this that allows one to be thus? After a long silence, he said: "With gold and jade, there is shared laughter; without rice and firewood, [there is nothing]."
Everyone knit their brows.
He ascended the hall and said, "Baoning remembers a particularly extraordinary koan from thirty years ago that I wish to present to the assembly.
Yet, by the time I reached the Dharma Hall, I had forgotten both the story and the very crux of the case itself. Is there anyone here who still remembers it?"
"Try to bring it up," he said. The assembly had no reply. The Master said, "It is found in great abundance south of the Yangtze, but is utterly absent north of the river.
He ascended the hall and said: "A peck cannot measure it; a scale can weigh it. Half of it is yet complete; it has a head but no tail.
Tell me, what thing is this?"
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Baoning’s food is coarse and poor; there are no other refined or exquisite delicacies to offer you all.
Now that you have arrived here, when opening your mats and spreading your bowls, you must be able to eat this tasteless fare before you may succeed.
If you cannot eat it, do not take offense."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Long? A thousand sages cannot measure it. Short? It does not even fit within the eye of a gnat.
He struck the ground once and said: "Last night there was rain upon the river; it has divided into the currents of ten thousand households."
Ascending the hall, he said: "What is this? Why is it so difficult to understand? What is this? Why is it so easy to comprehend? Do you truly understand?
It is not that those who are not enemies do not gather together."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If you wish to enter the ocean of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), you must board the boat of Prajñā. Holding up his staff, he said: "This here is the ocean of non-action;
which one is the boat of Prajñā? Throwing down the staff, he said: "Observe this skillful means well; take care not to drift away and fall into the land of the rākṣasas."

Ascending the hall: Auspicious snow falls at the end of the last month of winter; a gentle breeze arises in early spring. With an empty heart, I shall express my longing for home to those who are about to travel.
This longing for home knows no taboos; to those about to travel, who are distant and who are kin?
Circling Mount Sumeru a hundred thousand times, one does not know where, in the end, to hide one’s body. (He slaps the meditation seat. Descending from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Upon this lump of red flesh is the true person of no station. Eight *liang* in the left eye, half a *jin* in the right eye.
Buying high and selling low—gold and silver.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "I have a mouth, within which lies a tongue three inches long. My teeth are all complete, and there is no matter of right or wrong that I do not speak of.
Zhaozhou’s wooden Buddha emits radiance; Shaoshi’s iron ox has its two horns broken. He struck the meditation seat and descended from the hall.

Ascending the hall, he raised the case: When Zhaozhou was approaching the end of his life, he ordered a monk to carry his whisk and deliver a message to the Prince of Zhao, saying, "This is something this old monk has used throughout his entire life and will never exhaust.
He then said, "That Zhaozhou spent his whole life using it without exhausting it shows that his final entrustment was not mistaken.
Yet, although the entrustment was not mistaken, one cannot help but wonder why the Prince of Zhao could not lift it up. He then took up his staff and said:
"This is what Baoning used throughout his entire life and never exhausted. Rather than keeping it to himself, before he dies he hands it out equally with both hands to everyone.
He threw down his staff, clapped his hands, and said, "A-la-la! After thirty years, do not let it be lost!"
Ascending the hall: The spring colors are exquisite and lovely; the spring sunlight is radiant and glorious. The myriad people sing and rejoice; the hundred birds clamor and call.

Everywhere the grass is spread like carpets; at every household’s gate, green and red banners cluster together. The pavilions and halls rise in towering majesty; the wine shops and tea houses wind along in winding curves.
Whether man or woman, regardless of rank—be they young men or maidens—they come two by two and three by three, walking and singing as they go.
Sometimes they carry flowers with a smile; sometimes they pluck willow branches while knitting their brows. Here they shake their heads; there they clap their hands.
Acting foolish and acting dazed, appearing as if mad or deranged—if suddenly someone were to catch sight of them coldly, they would surely become a great object of ridicule.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Since I first fell ill and have lain in bed for this summer at Baoning, I have been voiding excrement and urine within the abbot’s quarters, babbling and talking in my sleep;
I truly could not distinguish east from west nor south from north. I sought life but did not live, and I sought death but did not die."
"At such a time as this, is there anyone who can rescue you? If there is, where do you apply your effort?
If there is not, Baoning will simply fall down by myself. [He] struck the meditation bench and descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Not seeing a single dharma is the Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara. Where is this Avalokiteśvara?
When you realize it, karmic obstacles are originally empty. What do you realize? If you have not yet realized it, you must still repay your past debts."
What is it that you have not yet understood? If you can penetrate through this point, then there is no hindrance as you walk east or west upon level ground.
If you cannot penetrate through, then the heavenly net is vast and wide—loose, yet nothing escapes it.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The outflow-free, true purity—how could anything else be admitted within it? He let out a shout, struck the meditation seat once, and said:
"Such a fine person refuses to act as one; they insist on lying in excrement."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When seeing the act of seeing, that which sees is not itself seeing. Seeing is already detached from seeing; seeing cannot reach it.
He struck the meditation staff and asked, "Do you see yet? "The setting clouds and solitary wild ducks fly together; the autumn waters and the vast sky share one color."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The path of the Buddha is long and distant; only after enduring diligent suffering for a long time can it be perfected.

Yet there is someone who does not undergo diligent suffering, who does not traverse the passage of long or short duration, who neither acts as a sentient being nor becomes a Buddha. Now tell me, has this person attained ultimate realization or not?
After a long silence, he said: "Do not cause him to remain stuck."

Ascending the hall, he said: "It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised. Its essence is like empty space, without shore or limit. Without departing from its present location, it is ever serene and still.
If you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen. Do you see it? When one’s affairs are few, afflictions are few;
where one knows many people, disputes are many."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To be able to speak but unable to practice—who is that? To be able to practice but unable to speak—how truly marvelous!
One step, one snap of the fingers; one nod, one frown. He struck the meditation seat and called to the assembly: "A purple sandalwood stupa of seven or eight tiers;
red lotus flowers of three or four branches."
Ascending the hall, Dongshan said: "On the summit of Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the Buddha Hall, it is a 'dog-urine sky. At the top of the bannerpole, a pestle is being fried;
three monkeys toss coins at night. Shishuang said: "The wind blows through the stone mortar, which once roared;
a clay-gnashed yakṣa runs through the void. Kicking over the moon in the sea, chaotic waves arise; startled, the earth..."
"A star invades the Southern Dipper. Daowu said: "A three-faced wildcat grasps the moon with its paws; a two-headed white ox seizes the mist with its hooves.
A crowned green hare stands upon the courtyard cypress; a shelled tortoise flies up into the heavens. The Master said: "These are the three verses."
First, it serves as a teacher for the patriarchs and Buddhas; second, it is a test for the eyes of the patch-robed monks; third, it serves as a signpost for all people under heaven.
If one can definitively grasp this, they may be said to possess a single eye.
Ascending the hall: The ancestral style of the Buddhas is displayed and unfolded according to the occasion; the livelihood of the patch-robed monks is spread abroad everywhere.

Plowing the earth to open fields, reaping grain and cutting grass, lighting fires and selecting vegetables, carrying water and hauling firewood, brewing vinegar and buying oil, begging for money and holding the alms bowl, rowing the boat with oars, pulling stones and pushing carts—these eighty thousand subtle practices constitute their adornment, and these three thousand codes of conduct are their ritual observances.

Fully endowed [with these qualities], he turned the Wheel of Dharma atop Mount Jiakui and proclaimed the secret intent within lands as minute as motes of dust. The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages were utterly bewildered;
the Śrāvakas of the Four Fruits were completely at a loss. Leaning his staff across his shoulder, he asked, "Is there anyone who can say it? The assembly remained silent.
The Master said, "When you are ready to bring forth your hand, you must bring it forth; when you have found a place to hide your body, you may hide there."
[The Master] strikes the sounding block once and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall: Xu You washed his ears to sell his purity and loftiness; Chao Fu fed his oxen to feign a display of magnanimity.

Tai Gong dangled his fishing line, yet he still harbored a purpose; Fan Li sailed upon the lake, yet how could he truly leave no trace? Only when ruler and subject find harmony in the Way can it be so.
The rivers and seas are tranquil and clear; the wind does not rustle the branches, and the rain does not break the clods of earth.

How can this compare to the wild flowers blooming everywhere in the third month, or the yellow leaves filling the void as they fly in the ninth autumn? Singing wildly before the azure caves, I am deeply intoxicated within the jade pitcher.
Clapping my hands and laughing loudly, I ask: "Do you know? Yesterday was the cold frost of late autumn; today is—"
It is a slight chill in the early winter. Ascending the hall:
the night is still and the moon is bright; the water is clear and the fish appear. A single cast of the golden hook—where shall one seek its tracks?
Raising his staff, he says: "Examine it closely, examine it closely."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally silent and vast.
It can act as the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet it does not wither along with the four seasons. Holding up his staff, he said: "For now, do not call this a 'walking staff'."
Elder Shouning ascends the hall to give his discourse: "A single night at Caoxi was truly quite senseless; Huangbo’s three blows were merely mutual neglect.
The meditation cushions and Zen boards have oppressed the person within. To ask for fire to burn them—this would still be somewhat better."
"Today, Baoning has no other way to see off Elder Shouning," he said. Taking up his staff, he declared, "I have only this single black-lacquered staff;
I shall not conceal it further. Before the great assembly, I entrust it to you with both hands. He threw down the staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A great man! His features are coarse and plain. East, west, south, north—where can he be constrained? His spirit pierces the universe; he sits and cuts off Vairocana.
Furthermore, what need is there to speak of that blue-eyed barbarian who came from the West?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "My mind is like the autumn moon; its radiance is bright and pure within the azure pool. There is nothing with which it can be compared—how am I to describe it?
Han Shanzi, you sell your priceless spirit for a low price! Consider this carefully: for what reason do you act thus?"
"Even so, thirty years from now, there will be someone who comes to investigate whether Baoning is still here.
He ascended the hall and said: "The karma-mirror stands before him; the thief’s identity is already exposed. Since the stolen goods are right there in plain sight, why does he refuse to confess?
Do you understand? Three thousand blows in the morning, eight hundred blows in the evening!"
He went out and returned to the hall. The frosty wind howls and the leaves fall in profusion. At dawn he enters the door of an old villager in a deep village.
Upon meeting, they simply sit together in silence; there is nothing at all to discuss. After a long while, he said: "It is easy to enter the mountains and capture a tiger."
It is difficult to open one's mouth toward others.
Ascending the hall, he pressed both hands against his knees and said, "Upon this ball of red flesh, it stands ten thousand fathoms high. He let out a shout and descended from the seat.
The Verse on the Ancient:
When the World-Honored One was first born, he walked seven steps, gazed in the four directions, pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward the earth, and said:
"In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am the most honored."
Before chaos was divided, no one understood; as heaven and earth were first split apart, things manifested in hidden splendor. Nature’s innate skill is truly strange;
in the end, it yields to him for a final performance.
A non-Buddhist asked the Buddha, "I do not ask regarding words of existence, nor do I ask regarding words of non-existence. The World-Honored One remained seated as he was.

After the non-Buddhist had prostrated and offered praise, saying, "The World-Honored One, with great kindness and great compassion, has cleared away my clouds of delusion and enabled me to enter," he departed.
Later, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "What principle did that non-Buddhist perceive that he prostrated, offered praise, and then left?"
The Master said: "It is like a fine horse that moves at the mere sight of the whip's shadow.
Having traveled on, he encountered night and stayed overnight in the wild grasses. When he opened his eyes, the sky was already bright with dawn.
With an empty mind and bare feet, he returned singing; by then, the travelers on the road were already many."
The rishi with five supernormal powers asked the World-Honored One, "I possess five supernormal powers; the Buddha possesses six.

What is this one supernormal power? The World-Honored One then called out to the rishi with five supernormal powers, and the rishi responded. The World-Honored One said, "That one supernormal power—you ask me about it."
Never encountered before throughout immeasurable kalpas—how can you remain unmoving and yet arrive within it? Do not say that the Buddha-dharma is but a trifle;
how could Gautama, who suffers most, have attained even a single penetration?
One day, while the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower to show the multitude. Kāśyapa smiled.
The World-Honored One said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye; I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. You must now propagate this teaching so that it does not come to an end."
Our Buddha held up a flower on Mount Ling; the ascetic Kāśyapa suddenly broke into a smile.
With his golden mouth, he secretly entrusted this secret teaching, not only to those in heaven but to those among men as well.
Mañjuśrī ordered Sudhana to enter the mountains to gather medicinal herbs. Mañjuśrī said, "Bring back whatever is not medicine.
Sudhana replied, "In these mountains, there is nothing that is not medicine. Mañjuśrī said, "Then bring back whatever is medicine.
Sudhana picked up a single blade of grass from the ground and handed it to Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī received it and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This medicine..."
It can kill, and it can also bring life.
The people of this vast earth are as sick as flax; the auspicious, numinous medicine reveals itself boundlessly.
Yet, amidst this, death and life are difficult to distinguish—this merely adds further flowers before one's eyes.
Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe, what else did the World-Honored One transmit? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda!
Ānanda responded, "Yes? Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate."
Where the Elephant King has trodden, the tracks of foxes vanish; his noble offspring continue this tradition. Need one speak of what will happen two thousand years hence?
Even through kalpas as vast as dust motes and sands, how could it ever come to an end?
King Aśoka asked Piṇḍola: "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha; is this true?
He parted his eyebrows with both hands and said, "I personally saw the Buddha."
Our Buddha personally beheld Piṇḍola: his eyebrows were long, his hair short, and his two eyes coarse.
King Aśoka still harbored doubts like a fox. Oṃ māṇidāri siri sulu.
Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty asked Bodhidharma, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? Dharma replied, "Vast emptiness;
there is no sage. The Emperor asked, "Who is it that stands before me? Dharma replied, "I do not know."
Heated until glowing red, struck with a single hammer-blow—countless sparks fly about in every direction. A perfect ten out of ten, this diamond-hard vajra;
spread it out before the gate, to whom shall it be sold?
One day Bodhidharma said, "I shall not remain in this world for long. Who among you has attained my true Dharma? Come forward, and I will provide witness for you.
Dao Fu said, "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, yet I do not depart from them;

I take this as the functioning of the Way. Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my skin. The nun Zongchi said, "What I now understand is like the joy [of a child]. Bodhidharma said, "You have attained my flesh."
Huiyi gazed upon the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; having seen it once, he saw it no more. Sengmo said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist. In the place where I see, there is truly not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind.
Sengmo said, "You have obtained my bones. The Second Patriarch stepped forward, prostrated three times, and stood in his place. Sengmo—
It is said: "You have attained my marrow.
Before the gate, the sons stand in ranks, each displaying his heroism as he surpasses the King of Wu. How is it that there is one alone who remains silent?
He sits, cutting off all opposition, as invincible as Vairocana.
The Sixth Patriarch saw two monks disputing over the wind and the banner; one said, "The wind moves," and the other said, "The banner moves.
The Patriarch said, "It is not the wind that moves; it is not the banner that moves."
Vast and expansive is this imperial post road; morning and night, it has never barred the passage of people.
It is not that my entire family fails to advance, but alas, thorns have grown before our very door.
The Sixth Patriarch asked Master Rang, "Where have you come from? Rang replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What thing is it that comes like this?
Rang replied, "To describe it as a single thing is not to the point. The Patriarch said, "Is there still any need for cultivation and realization?
Rang replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent, yet one must not be defiled by them. The Patriarch said, "This very state of being undefiled is it."
"The Buddhas protect and mind them; I am likewise so, and you are likewise so. Thus prophesied by the twenty-seventh patriarch of the Western Heaven, Prajñātāra:
"After you, there shall emerge a colt that will trample the people of the world underfoot."
Horns upon his head and fur upon his back, he comes thus; the Iron Ring Mountains and all peaks are shattered asunder. He tramples the Jambudvīpa continent until countless people are killed;
his nose is pierced deeply through, and he cannot be pulled back.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he could not attain the Way of Buddhahood.

When the three periods of time are severed, both ordinary beings and sages are exhausted; when the ten bodies are perfected, they pervade the atoms of all lands. Responding to things without partiality, they accord with the heights [of capacity]."
[This refers to] the lower [grade]. It is cultivated for the duration of many *asaṃkhyeya* great kalpas.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "He who gives to you is not called a field of merit; he who makes offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms."
Boundless and limitless, there is no need for deliberation; with the ebb and flow of the tide, all is inherently level.
Whether clear or turbid, shallow or deep, bitter or bland—the single flavor is distinct and clear.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All worthy sages are distinguished by means of the dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
When the benevolent see it, they call it benevolence; when the wise see it, they call it wisdom. In cold weather one turns toward the fire; in heat one seeks the cool breeze.
When vigorous, one practices walking meditation (*caṅkrama*); when weary, one sleeps. When weary and sleeping, one looks up at the sky, opens the mouth to take in breath."
The pure practitioner does not enter nirvana; the precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell.
Throughout his life he was carefree and unrestrained, wandering at will through wine shops and tea houses. Neither the Han land took him in nor the Qin state looked after him;
moreover, he rode his donkey past Yangzhou.
Master Si instructed Shitou to go to the place of Master Nanyue Huairang. He sent a letter saying, "When you return, I will give you a hoe for dwelling in a hermitage.
Shitou then went to Huairang’s place and asked, "What is it like when one seeks neither the various sages nor values one's own spiritual nature?
Huairang said, "Your question is far too lofty. Why not ask about things below? Shitou—
Dongshan said, "Would you rather sink into the depths for eternal kalpas and not seek the liberation of the sages? He then turned and reflected, saying, "Did your son deliver the letter?

Touzi replied, "The letter was not received, nor did the message reach him. Dongshan continued, "Yesterday I was honored by the Master’s permission for you to dwell in the hermitage with the 'Tao-axe.
You may request it now. Dongshan lowered one foot, and Touzi immediately prostrated himself.
From of old, the ancestors have served as sovereigns; son after son, generation after generation, they have flourished. None among the civil and military officials recognize them;
they must surely have a venerable hall within the Golden Palace.
Mazu was sitting in meditation. Huairang asked him, "What do you intend to accomplish by sitting in meditation? Mazu replied, "I intend to become a Buddha. Huairang stopped there.
On the following day, Huairang instead began rubbing a brick against a stone near Mazu’s seat. Mazu asked, "What do you intend to accomplish by rubbing this brick?
Huairang replied, "I intend to make a mirror. Mazu said, "How can you make a mirror by rubbing a brick? Huairang said, "Rubbing a brick..."
"If you do not act as a mirror, how can you attain Buddhahood through seated meditation? The Patriarch asked, "Ultimately, what do you instruct me to do?
Xiang replied, "It is like using an ox to pull a cart. If the cart does not move, is it right to beat the cart, or is it right to beat the ox?
The Patriarch then attained realization.
The "dead horse doctor" has come; there is no place for him to be of use. A whip is added to the hindquarters of the oxen. Does he know that the skin is pierced and the flesh is torn?
To bear a heavy burden, one must surely possess full strength of limb.
Baizhang went for his second audience with Mazu. When Mazu saw him coming, he pointed to the whisk at the corner of the meditation seat.
Baizhang said, "Is it used right here, or is it used apart from this? Mazu said, "When you open your mouth in the future, what will you have to offer people?
Baizhang took up the whisk and held it upright. Mazu said, "Is it used right here, or is it used apart from this? Baizhang hung the whisk back on its original place.
At that moment, the Patriarch let out a shout, which left Baizhang deaf for three days.
A wooden horse tramples the people of Jambudvīpa to death; a clay dragon drinks dry the waters of the vast ocean. Thunder fills the sky and mountains crumble;
look, and waves rise from the level plain.
Master Pang asked Mazu, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as his companion?
Mazu replied, "Wait until you can swallow all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I will tell you."
The wind blows and the sun scorches as exposed corpses lie; weeping, I ask the mountain man for a place to bury them. This old man with too many words cannot restrain his impatience;
there is no place where yin and yang can be arranged.
Master Pang asked Mazu, "The original body is not obscure; I ask the Master to cast his eyes high. Mazu looked directly down at him.
The Master said, "A single-stringed lute; only you, Master, can play it wondrously. Mazu looked directly up at him. Master Pang bowed.
As Mazu returned to his quarters, Master Pang followed behind him and said, "Seeking skillfulness, one ends up with clumsiness."

Lifted up, it all comes down to but a single spark; suddenly it leaps into flames, stretching across the sky until dawn. Spreading across the wilds, it is still difficult to extinguish;

The snow-blade contains light that shoots toward the Dipper and Ox; not only do Heaven, Earth, ghosts, and spirits grieve. The life-root has fallen into Nanquan’s hand;

The head of the wildcat has grown horns anew; the old man Wang walks alone at night before his gate. Dawn breaks and he knows not where he has gone;

Last night at the third watch, I lost my ox; at dawn, having risen, I have lost my fire. My belt is not yet fastened and my shoes are not yet on;

Softly wrapping his blade, he enters the fray; at the moment of capture, his eyes stare wide open. A hero who decides life and death in a single stroke;

Dayu asked, "What words or phrases did Huangbo say recently? Nanquan recounted the previous conversation and asked, "I do not know where my fault lies."

Ji descended from his meditation seat, grabbed the monk, and said, "Speak! Speak! The monk hesitated. Ji pushed him away and said, "What is this?
Stirring up dust and scattering soil—nowhere to hide. Entering and exiting through the face-gate like a great wolf. Spilling urine and excrement is but a trivial matter;
in the vast flow, who can distinguish the foul from the fragrant?"

Sansheng replied, "How would I dare? Linji asked, "If someone were to ask you, what would you say?
Sansheng then gave a shout. Linji said, "Who knew that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished by such a blind donkey!"
He then uttered a verse: "Following the current without ceasing, one asks: 'How is this? True illumination is boundless; I shall explain it to you.
